logline: A young blind woman resurfaces after seven years missing - now able to see and calling herself 'The OA' - and draws a small group of strangers into a mythology of near-death experiences, captivity, and interdimensional travel.

seasons.review_body: Part I of The OA arrived on Netflix in December 2016 with almost no advance publicity, and the secrecy served it. Critics split on whether its ambitions were genuine or pretentious: the 76% Rotten Tomatoes score from 68 reviews reflected real division. Variety found the narrative collapsed under scrutiny; Vox's Emily St. James called it 'kind of genius, while simultaneously being incredibly silly.' The consensus praised Brit Marling's performance and the show's formal boldness - near-death experiences rendered as embodied choreography, mythology built with genuine imaginative commitment. The finale's climactic sequence generated more debate than perhaps any single scene that year. Part I is best approached as a provocation rather than a puzzle: the feelings it generates are real even where the logic isn't watertight.

episode_reviews.title: Homecoming
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes The OA's tone immediately - elliptical, earnest, committed to its own strange logic. A woman jumps off a bridge and walks back into the world with new eyes. The show trusts that image to carry the first hour.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Prairie's eyes opening after the jump - a simple image that announces the show's refusal to play by conventional mystery rules.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Oa S01E01: "Homecoming" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The woman in the hospital has already been named before she names herself. Alice says she is a nurse. Others insist the injured person is Prairie Johnson. The room tries to solve her with paperwork, concern, and the relief of recognition. Then the body on the bed pushes back with one small sentence: "I'm the OA." That is the hour's cleanest move. "Homecoming" begins with return, then makes return feel like another kind of capture. The premiere works because it treats identity as a fight over control, even when its recruitment machinery starts to run ahead of the feeling.

## A Name Is the First Cage

**Prairie** enters the episode as a person other people already think they understand. That is the cruelty built into the homecoming. Her name is asserted, her injury is processed, her sudden ability to see becomes a public miracle, and the people around her try to fold the impossible into something manageable. The episode's smartest choice is to make that management feel invasive.

The line that cuts through the early confusion is simple: "That is not your name." The correction is aimed outward, but it also teaches the hour how to move. Names are unstable here. Alice identifies herself. Prairie is identified by others. **the OA** identifies herself against the version being forced onto her. Later, the note that Broderick-Allen is a different person extends the same pressure. A name in this premiere is a claim on someone's story.

That gives the early scenes their charge. The crowd's praise of Prairie's supposed new sight should comfort her, but the writing frames it as another intrusion. Everyone wants to celebrate the result. The person at the center keeps resisting the terms. Home is offered like safety. The episode lets it feel like a room with too many hands reaching in.

The risk is obvious: withholding can become a pose. Here, for most of the opening stretch, it holds because the refusal is specific. The OA does more than behave mysteriously. She corrects, demands, rejects, and redirects. The mystery has verbs.

## The Internet Demand Turns Wonder Into Strategy

The episode gets sharper when the OA's behavior stops looking like pure trauma response and starts looking like strategy. When she demands Internet access from Prairie Johnson, the hour pivots from medical aftermath into active planning. She wants a password. She threatens departure. She is no longer only being handled by others. She is handling the room back.

That shift matters because it complicates sympathy without flattening it. The OA's fractured state, the back scarring implied by the open questions, and the claims about death could push the episode into one register: injured woman returns with impossible story. Instead, "Homecoming" gives her an agenda early. She needs access. She searches for **Homer**, less a present character than a gravitational pull, a connection strong enough to organize action from a distance.

This is the premiere's best craft instinct. It refuses to make the central figure passive. Even when surrounded by people who impose Prairie Johnson on her, the OA keeps creating conditions. She pushes for the tools she needs. She converts concern into leverage. The title promises homecoming, but the plotting behaves like escape planning.

The weakness sits beside the strength. Because the episode is built around refusals and conditions, the emotional ground can feel heavily withheld. That is a valid strategy with a cost. Some beats ask for investment before the hour has shown enough of the human bond beneath the mission. The spine is strong. The warmth is rationed hard.

## Five People at Midnight Is a Hook With Teeth

The "five people" demand at midnight gives the premiere its cleanest genre shape. Until then, the hour is a swirl of names, access, injury, and unease. With the midnight plan, the OA turns ambiguity into recruitment. She selects. She asks for a specific number, at a specific time, under a specific framing tied to "Strangers on the Train."

That precision is valuable. Vague mysticism is easy. A plan with logistics is harder to fake. The episode understands that a strange command becomes more compelling when it has procedure. Five people. Midnight. A journey to the border. Leave something important behind. These are ritual terms, but they are also plot terms. They give the episode a clock and a test.

The border language is especially useful because it lands in two registers. On one level, it suggests movement, crossing, departure. On another, it names the episode's larger obsession: borders between old name and new name, sight and blindness, death and return, private story and shared mission. The hour does not define it yet, and that withholding works because the term is attached to action. The characters are not sitting around admiring the mystery. The OA is making them move.

Still, the recruitment device arrives with a faint mechanical clang. The episode's emotional logic is built on violation and misnaming, then suddenly asks for a small ritual group to form around instructions. It is compelling, but abrupt. The hook has teeth. It also shows its hinges.

## The Backstory Begins as Instruction, Not Explanation

Near the end, the OA tells Prairie to close her eyes and imagine the story as if she is there. That choice is the premiere's key tonal turn. The episode stops circling the question of who she is in the present and begins moving into the story she wants to tell. Conversation becomes instruction. Memory becomes a guided experience.

The move could have been clumsy. Instead, the hour gives the narration a concrete starting point: Russia, Voi, dreams, and a town built on the fall. "Our town was built on the fall" is a strong foundation line because it ties fortune to disaster without overexplaining the mythology. It tells the viewer that the past will carry the same wound as the present: survival arriving with damage attached.

This is where the premiere's structure becomes clear. The hospital and home scenes train the viewer in how to listen. Names may be wrong. Sight may not bring clarity. Death may refuse a single meaning. A homecoming may be the least stable place in the story. By the time the monologue begins, the episode has earned the right to shift into legend because it has already made ordinary reality feel negotiable.

The risk remains restraint turning into opacity. The long, low-dialogue stretches help the atmosphere, but they also make certain emotional beats feel suspended rather than developed. The episode has confidence in silence. At times, it hides inside it.

## The Verdict

"Homecoming" is a strong premiere because it makes identity the battleground before mythology becomes the attraction. The OA's return is staged as an argument over who gets to name her, use her, believe her, and follow her. The hour works best when those pressures are practical: a demanded password, a corrected name, five people at midnight. It is less sturdy when the ritual mechanics arrive before the emotional circle has fully tightened.

Even so, the episode plants its open loops with discipline. Sight, scars, death, Homer, the border, and the fall all point toward a season built on crossings that should be impossible. BollyAI's score: 8.0/10. A strange, controlled opening with unanswered questions that keep changing what people do.

verdict.one_liner: A controlled, eerie premiere where names become weapons and the mystery works because it keeps forcing action.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Part I finale divides more than it resolves - the climactic sequence either lands as the most formally daring thing on streaming television that year or as an earnest absurdity, depending entirely on whether the show has earned your trust.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Five Movements sequence - the scene that generated more debate than any other TV moment in 2016.

bollymeter.basis: Part II earned 92% on Rotten Tomatoes as Marling and Batmanglij expanded the mythology with greater formal confidence and a genuinely surprising dimensional premise that won over many Part I sceptics.

pull_quotes.text: The first series was like nothing else.

seasons.review_body: Part II is the better half of The OA's truncated run. A 92% Rotten Tomatoes score from 38 critics reflected near-unanimous agreement that Marling and Batmanglij had sharpened their tools: the dimensional conceit expanded the show's world in directions that felt imaginatively earned rather than arbitrarily strange. Critics who had resisted Part I found easier entry points; the direction grew bolder and the mythology more coherent. The cancellation announcement arriving just months after Part II's release made the unresolved cliffhanger a particular wound for devoted audiences. As a statement about ambition, The OA's two parts together represent something genuinely singular in the Netflix catalogue: a show that willed its own mythology into existence and was cancelled before it could prove whether that mythology was architecture or ornament.
seasons.season_over_season: Part II surpasses Part I in formal confidence and critical consensus, expanding the mythology with greater structural coherence and directorial ambition.
